claim: Members of the Corynebacterineae suborder of Actinobacteria have a unique cell surface architecture.
source: Members of the Corynebacterineae  suborder of Actinobacteria have a unique cell surface architecture and, unlike most well-studied bacteria, grow by tip-extension.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characteristic of the Corynebacterineae suborder.

claim: Members of the Corynebacterineae suborder grow by tip-extension, unlike most well-studied bacteria.
source: Members of the Corynebacterineae  suborder of Actinobacteria have a unique cell surface architecture and, unlike most well-studied bacteria, grow by tip-extension.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a distinguishing feature of the Corynebacterineae.

claim: A high-density transposon mutagenized library of Corynebacterium glutamicum was challenged with a panel of antibiotics and other stresses.
source: A high-density transposon mutagenized library was challenged with a panel of antibiotics and other stresses.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The fitness of mutants in each gene under each condition was assessed by transposon-sequencing.
source: The fitness of mutants in each gene under each condition was then assessed by transposon-sequencing.
evidence: This describes the method used to evaluate mutant fitness.

claim: Clustering of phenotypic fingerprints revealed a role for several genes of previously unknown function in surface biogenesis.
source: Clustering of the resulting phenotypic fingerprints revealed a role for several genes of previously unknown function in surface biogenesis.
evidence: This is a key finding from the phenotypic profiling analysis.

claim: CofA (Cgp_0016) is an interaction partner of the peptidoglycan synthase PBP1a.
source: Further analysis identified CofA (Cgp_0016) as an interaction partner of the peptidoglycan synthase PBP1a that promotes its stable accumulation at sites of polar growth.
evidence: This is a major finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: CofA promotes stable accumulation of PBP1a at sites of polar growth.
source: Further analysis identified CofA (Cgp_0016) as an interaction partner of the peptidoglycan synthase PBP1a that promotes its stable accumulation at sites of polar growth.
evidence: This describes the functional role of CofA in relation to PBP1a.

claim: The related Mycobacterium tuberculosis CofA and PBP1a proteins interact.
source: The related Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins were also found to interact, highlighting the utility of our dataset for uncovering conserved principles of morphogenesis for this clinically relevant bacterial suborder.
evidence: This demonstrates conservation of the CofA-PBP1a interaction across species.

claim: Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis belong to the Corynebacterineae suborder of Actinobacteria.
source: Several medically important pathogens belong to the Corynebacterineae suborder of Actinobacteria, including Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation support.

claim: Corynebacterineae bacteria surround their cytoplasmic membrane with an essential cell wall matrix made of peptidoglycan.
source: Like most bacteria, these organisms surround their cytoplasmic membrane with an essential cell wall matrix made of the heteropolymer peptidoglycan (PG).
evidence: This describes a common feature of bacterial cell walls.

claim: Corynebacterineae bacteria uniquely modify the PG layer with an additional polysaccharide made of arabinan and galactan chains.
source: However, they uniquely modify the PG layer with an additional polysaccharide made of arabinan and galactan chains (Kieser and Rubin, 2014; Alderwick et al., 2015; Daffé and Marrakchi, 2019).
evidence: This describes a unique feature of Corynebacterineae cell walls, supported by citations.

claim: The arabinogalactan layer is further modified by glycolipids called mycolic acids, forming a second membrane.
source: This arabinogalactan (AG) layer is further modified by glycolipids called mycolic acids, forming a second membrane that is thought to function analogously to the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria (Kieser and Rubin, 2014; Alderwick et al., 2015; Daffé and Marrakchi, 2019).
evidence: This describes the structure of the mycolata cell envelope, supported by citations.

claim: The mycolata outer membrane is thought to function analogously to the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: This arabinogalactan (AG) layer is further modified by glycolipids called mycolic acids, forming a second membrane that is thought to function analogously to the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria (Kieser and Rubin, 2014; Alderwick et al., 2015; Daffé and Marrakchi, 2019).
evidence: This is a functional comparison supported by citations.

claim: Compounds that target mycolata cell envelope biogenesis are important components of current drug cocktails used to treat Mtb infections.
source: The overall envelope architecture of these bacteria is referred to as the mycolata cell envelope, and compounds that target its biogenesis are important components of current drug cocktails used to treat Mtb infections (Alderwick et al., 2015).
evidence: This highlights the clinical relevance of understanding mycolata envelope biogenesis, supported by citation.

claim: All Actinobacteria analyzed thus far grow by inserting new envelope material at their cell poles.
source: Like all other Actinobacteria analyzed thus far, members of the Corynebacterineae grow by inserting new envelope material at their cell poles (Flärdh, 2003; Daniel and Errington, 2003).
evidence: This describes a common growth mechanism in Actinobacteria, supported by citations.

claim: The DivIVA (Wag31) protein plays a key role in tip growth in Corynebacterineae.
source: The mechanisms that govern tip growth in these organisms are ill-defined, but the DivIVA (Wag31) protein has long been known to play a key role in the process (Flärdh, 2003; Letek et al., 2008; Nguyen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DivIVA function, supported by citations.

claim: DivIVA is thought to assemble into a cytoskeletal-like matrix lining the inner face of the cytoplasmic membrane at the cell poles.
source: This protein is thought to assemble into a cytoskeletal-like matrix lining the inner face of the cytoplasmic membrane at the cell poles (Edwards and Errington, 1997; Ramamurthi and Losick, 2009; Lenarcic et al., 2009; Oliva et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the proposed structural organization of DivIVA, supported by citations.

claim: DivIVA assemblies function by promoting the recruitment of cell envelope synthases to the pole.
source: Similar to FtsZ polymers that underly the cytokinetic ring, these DivIVA assemblies are believed to function by promoting the recruitment of cell envelope synthases to the pole where they can promote surface elongation (Kang et al., 2008; Melzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the proposed function of DivIVA assemblies, supported by citations.

claim: Both known classes of PG synthases have been found to localize to growing poles in several organisms.
source: Indeed, both known classes of PG synthases have been found to localize to growing poles in several organisms (Valbuena et al., 2007; Sieger et al., 2013; Sieger and Bramkamp, 2014; Hett et al., 2010; Kieser et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PG synthase localization, supported by citations.

claim: The two classes of PG synthases include bifunctional class A penicillin-binding proteins (aPBPs) and synthases composed of complexes formed between SEDS proteins and their class B PBP (bPBP) partners.
source: These synthases include the bifunctional class A penicillin-binding proteins (aPBPs) (Sauvage et al., 2008) and the relatively recently characterized synthases composed of complexes formed between SEDS proteins and their class B PBP (bPBP) partners (Meeske et al., 2016; Rohs et al., 2018; Taguchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the two classes of PG synthases, supported by citations.

claim: Phenotypic profiling has proven to be a useful strategy to identify phenotypes for genes of unknown function.
source: Phenotypic profiling has proven to be a useful strategy to identify phenotypes for genes of unknown function to help uncover their biological activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of phenotypic profiling.

claim: The phenotypic profiling method originally took advantage of the ordered knockout collections of yeast and Escherichia coli.
source: The method originally took advantage of the ordered knockout collections of yeast and Escherichia coli (Nichols et al., 2011; Hillenmeyer et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the historical development of phenotypic profiling, supported by citations.

claim: Similar phenotypic profiling approaches utilizing transposon-sequencing have recently been employed to generate profiles for several bacterial species.
source: Similar approaches utilizing transposon-sequencing have recently been employed to generate profiles for several bacterial species (Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018), but an extensive analysis has not yet been carried out in the Corynebacterineae.
evidence: This describes recent applications of transposon-sequencing for phenotypic profiling, supported by citations.

claim: An extensive phenotypic profiling analysis has not yet been carried out in the Corynebacterineae prior to this study.
source: Similar approaches utilizing transposon-sequencing have recently been employed to generate profiles for several bacterial species (Wetmore et al., 2015; Price et al., 2018), but an extensive analysis has not yet been carried out in the Corynebacterineae.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the current study.

claim: A Cglu transposon library of approximately 200,000 unique insertions was used for the phenotypic profiling analysis.
source: To generate phenotypic profiles, a Cglu transposon library of approximately 200,000 unique insertions was grown for eleven generations in the presence of drug or under a stress condition.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for the phenotypic profiling.

claim: The transposon library was grown for eleven generations in the presence of drug or under a stress condition.
source: To generate phenotypic profiles, a Cglu transposon library of approximately 200,000 unique insertions was grown for eleven generations in the presence of drug or under a stress condition.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for the phenotypic profiling.

claim: The best transposon-sequencing results were obtained when a drug concentration yielding a mild but observable decrease in growth rate was used.
source: For drug treatments, initial trials revealed that the best transposon-sequencing results were obtained when a drug concentration yielding a mild but observable decrease in growth rate was used.
evidence: This describes an optimization finding for the experimental protocol.

claim: Drug concentrations used were typically 1/4 to 1/2 the measured minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) for each drug.
source: Typically these concentrations were 1/4 to 1/2 the measured minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) for each drug (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the drug concentrations used, with reference to supplementary data.

claim: 40 different growth conditions were analyzed in the phenotypic profiling study.
source: All total, 40 different growth conditions were analyzed with the collection of drugs used spanning all major targets, including PG and AG biogenesis, DNA replication, transcription, and translation (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the scope of the phenotypic profiling analysis.

claim: The drugs used in the phenotypic profiling spanned all major targets, including PG and AG biogenesis, DNA replication, transcription, and translation.
source: All total, 40 different growth conditions were analyzed with the collection of drugs used spanning all major targets, including PG and AG biogenesis, DNA replication, transcription, and translation (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the diversity of drug targets used in the study.

claim: Replicates of untreated cultures resulted in highly correlated fitness scores for each gene.
source: Replicates of untreated cultures resulted in highly correlated fitness scores for each gene, with most genes yielding a fitness score near 1.0 as expected for such a comparison (Figure 1B).
evidence: This demonstrates the reproducibility of the experimental approach.

claim: Approximately 40% of all non-essential genes were found to have a moderate phenotype in at least one condition tested.
source: Overall, approximately 40% of all non-essential genes were found to have a moderate phenotype in at least one condition tested, indicated by a fitness score below 0.9 or above 1.1 (Figure 1C), with the vast majority of phenotypes observed being fitness defects.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding from the phenotypic profiling analysis.

claim: The vast majority of phenotypes observed in the phenotypic profiling were fitness defects.
source: Overall, approximately 40% of all non-essential genes were found to have a moderate phenotype in at least one condition tested, indicated by a fitness score below 0.9 or above 1.1 (Figure 1C), with the vast majority of phenotypes observed being fitness defects.
evidence: This describes the nature of the phenotypes observed.

claim: Genes encoding the two cytochrome d oxidase subunits (cydA and cydB) and cytochrome transporter (cydC and cydD) cluster tightly together in the phenotypic profiling analysis.
source: For example, genes encoding the two cytochrome d oxidase subunits (cydA and cydB) and cytochrome transporter (cydC and cydD) cluster tightly together, primarily due to their hypersensitivity to the benzothiazinone BTZ043 (Figure 2).
evidence: This demonstrates that the clustering accurately identifies functionally related genes.

claim: Genes encoding cytochrome d oxidase subunits and cytochrome transporter are hypersensitive to the benzothiazinone BTZ043.
source: For example, genes encoding the two cytochrome d oxidase subunits (cydA and cydB) and cytochrome transporter (cydC and cydD) cluster tightly together, primarily due to their hypersensitivity to the benzothiazinone BTZ043 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the phenotypic profiling analysis.

claim: There are synergistic effects between electron transport chain inhibitors and benzothiazinones against Mtb.
source: This finding is consistent with published literature demonstrating synergistic effects between electron transport chain inhibitors and benzothiazinones against Mtb (Lechartier and Cole, 2015).
evidence: This is cited literature that supports the observed phenotype.

claim: Genes encoding RipC, FtsE, and FtsX proteins cluster together in the phenotypic profiling analysis.
source: Additionally, genes encoding RipC, FtsE, and FtsX proteins that together form a complex required for proper cell wall remodeling at the division site (Lim et al., 2019; Tsuge et al., 2008; Maeda et al., 2016) were also found to have correlated profiles (Figure 2).
evidence: This demonstrates that the clustering identifies components of known protein complexes.

claim: RipC, FtsE, and FtsX proteins form a complex required for proper cell wall remodeling at the division site.
source: Additionally, genes encoding RipC, FtsE, and FtsX proteins that together form a complex required for proper cell wall remodeling at the division site (Lim et al., 2019; Tsuge et al., 2008; Maeda et al., 2016) were also found to have correlated profiles (Figure 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RipC-FtsE-FtsX complex, supported by citations.

claim: The phenotypic profiling analysis successfully differentiated the biological function of genes from the same genetic locus.
source: Another notable feature of the profiling analysis is that it successfully differentiated the biological function of genes from the same genetic locus.
evidence: This highlights a strength of the phenotypic profiling approach.

claim: Genes in the putative cgp_3163–3168 operon clustered into two distinct groups based on their functions.
source: For example, genes in the putative cgp_3163–3168 operon clustered into two distinct groups.
evidence: This is an example demonstrating functional differentiation within an operon.

claim: Mutants in cgp_3163, cgp_3165, cgp_3166, and cgp_3168 have been associated with defects in trehalose mycolate transport across the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Mutants in four of these genes (cgp_3163, cgp_3165, cgp_3166, and cgp_3168) have been associated with defects in trehalose mycolate transport across the cytoplasmic membrane (Yamaryo-Botte et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these genes, supported by citation.

claim: Mutants in cgp_3164 and mptA (cgp_2385) have a defect in the elongation of the mannan backbone of membrane glycolipids.
source: Gene cgp_3164 from this locus, on the other hand, was previously implicated in a different function. Mutants in this gene along with the unlinked mptA (cgp_2385) gene were found to have a defect in the elongation of the mannan backbone of membrane glycolipids (Cashmore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these genes, supported by citation.

claim: cgp_3164 clusters with mptA (cgp_2385) in the phenotypic profiling analysis.
source: Consistent with this finding, cgp_3164 clusters with mptA (cgp_2385) in our analysis and has a phenotypic profile distinct from its neighboring genes in the cgp_3163–3168 locus (Figure 2).
evidence: This demonstrates that the clustering reflects functional relationships rather than just genomic organization.

claim: The putative cgp_3012–3020 operon displayed specific hypersensitivity to bacitracin and vancomycin.
source: For example, the putative cgp_3012–3020 operon stood out due to the specific hypersensitivity to bacitracin and vancomycin displayed by mutants in all of its genes except for cgp_3015 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the phenotypic profiling analysis.

claim: Deletion of the entire cgp_3012–3020 locus or individual genes (cgp_3018 or cgp_3019) confirmed hypersensitivity to bacitracin and vancomycin.
source: This hypersensitivity was confirmed by deletion of the entire locus or individual genes (cgp_3018 or cgp_3019) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This validates the phenotypic profiling results with targeted deletions.

claim: Strains with deletions in the cgp_3012–3020 locus have a slight growth advantage on meropenem.
source: Also consistent with the phenotypic screen, these strains have a slight growth advantage on meropenem, but are not altered in their susceptibility to other drugs like ampicillin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is a specific phenotype observed for these deletion strains.

claim: Vancomycin acts by directly binding the lipid II precursor for PG synthesis.
source: Vancomycin acts by directly binding the lipid II precursor for PG synthesis, which consists of the lipid carrier undecaprenol pyrophosphate (Und-PP) linked with the dissacharide pentapeptide monomeric unit of PG (Reynolds, 1989; Schneider and Sahl, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about vancomycin's mechanism of action, supported by citations.

claim: Bacitracin targets the lipid stage of PG biogenesis by blocking the dephosphorylation of Und-PP products.
source: Bacitracin similarly targets the lipid stage of PG biogenesis by blocking the dephosphorylation of Und-PP products of PG glycan polymerases such that Und-P is not regenerated for use in the synthesis of lipid II, causing PG synthesis to be inhibited (Schneider and Sahl, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacitracin's mechanism of action, supported by citation.

claim: The specific hypersensitivity of mutants in the cgp_3012–3020 locus to drugs that interfere with lipid II biogenesis suggests this cluster may be involved in undecaprenol synthesis or utilization.
source: Thus, the specific hypersensitivity of mutants in the cgp_3012–3020 locus to drugs that interfere with lipid II biogenesis suggests that this large uncharacterized cluster of genes may be involved in undecaprenol synthesis or utilization to facilitate proper cell surface assembly in Cglu.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed drug sensitivities.

claim: The cofA gene encodes a small membrane protein of 114 amino acids with two predicted transmembrane domains and an N-in/C-in topology.
source: The cofA gene encodes a small membrane protein of 114 amino acids with two predicted transmembrane domains and an N-in/C-in topology (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the structural features of CofA based on sequence analysis.

claim: The phenotypic profile of cofA clustered tightly with the ponA gene encoding PBP1a.
source: Its phenotypic profile clustered tightly with the ponA gene (Figure 3A) (correlation coefficient 0.91) encoding PBP1a, an aPBP-type synthase that helps build the PG layer.
evidence: This is a key finding from the phenotypic profiling analysis.

claim: The correlation coefficient between cofA and ponA phenotypic profiles is 0.91.
source: Its phenotypic profile clustered tightly with the ponA gene (Figure 3A) (correlation coefficient 0.91) encoding PBP1a, an aPBP-type synthase that helps build the PG layer.
evidence: This quantifies the similarity between cofA and ponA phenotypic profiles.

claim: PBP1a is an aPBP-type synthase that helps build the PG layer.
source: Its phenotypic profile clustered tightly with the ponA gene (Figure 3A) (correlation coefficient 0.91) encoding PBP1a, an aPBP-type synthase that helps build the PG layer.
evidence: This describes the function of PBP1a.

claim: PBP1a is a bitopic membrane protein with a small N-terminal cytoplasmic domain, a single transmembrane helix, and a large extracellular region.
source: Like other aPBPs, PBP1a is a bitopic membrane protein with a small N-terminal cytoplasmic domain, a single transmembrane helix, and a large extracellular region (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the structural organization of PBP1a.

claim: The extracellular portion of PBP1a contains both a glycosyltransferase (GTase, polymerase) domain and a transpeptidase (TPase) domain.
source: The extracellular portion of the synthase contains both a glycosyltransferase (GTase, polymerase) domain that polymerizes lipid II into PG glycans and a transpeptidase (TPase) domain that forms the crosslinks between peptides of adjacent PG glycans in the wall matrix (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the functional domains of PBP1a.

claim: The GTase domain of PBP1a polymerizes lipid II into PG glycans.
source: The extracellular portion of the synthase contains both a glycosyltransferase (GTase, polymerase) domain that polymerizes lipid II into PG glycans and a transpeptidase (TPase) domain that forms the crosslinks between peptides of adjacent PG glycans in the wall matrix (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the function of the GTase domain.

claim: The TPase domain of PBP1a forms crosslinks between peptides of adjacent PG glycans in the wall matrix.
source: The extracellular portion of the synthase contains both a glycosyltransferase (GTase, polymerase) domain that polymerizes lipid II into PG glycans and a transpeptidase (TPase) domain that forms the crosslinks between peptides of adjacent PG glycans in the wall matrix (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the function of the TPase domain.

claim: Cglu encodes a second aPBP called PBP1b.
source: Cglu encodes a second aPBP called PBP1b, but its corresponding gene ponB (cgp_3313) had a phenotypic profile that was distinct from cofA and ponA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes another aPBP in Cglu.

claim: The ponB gene (cgp_3313) encoding PBP1b had a phenotypic profile that was distinct from cofA and ponA.
source: Cglu encodes a second aPBP called PBP1b, but its corresponding gene ponB (cgp_3313) had a phenotypic profile that was distinct from cofA and ponA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This demonstrates specificity of the cofA-ponA relationship.

claim: ΔponA cells displayed hypersensitivity to ampicillin and meropenem relative to wild-type cells.
source: As expected, ΔponA cells displayed hypersensitivity to ampicillin and meropenam relative to wild-type cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This validates the phenotypic profiling results with targeted deletions.

claim: Cells deleted for cofA showed similar sensitivity to ampicillin and meropenem as ΔponA cells, but the sensitivity defect was less severe.
source: Cells deleted for cofA showed a similar sensitivity to these drugs, but in both cases the sensitivity defect was less severe than that of ΔponA cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This demonstrates a phenotypic similarity between cofA and ponA deletions.

claim: Double ΔponA ΔcofA mutants displayed a drug sensitivity phenotype identical to the single ΔponA mutant.
source: Double ΔponA ΔcofA mutants displayed a drug sensitivity phenotype identical to the single ΔponA mutant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This suggests that cofA and ponA function in the same pathway.

claim: The reduced severity of the phenotypes for CofA inactivation relative to PBP1a inactivation suggests that PBP1a retains some residual function in the absence of CofA.
source: Thus, the mutant phenotypes of cells inactivated for PBP1a and CofA are indeed similar. However, the reduced severity of the phenotypes for CofA inactivation relative to PBP1a inactivation suggests that PBP1a retains some residual function in the absence of CofA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of mutant phenotypes.

claim: CofA promotes normal PBP1a function but is not absolutely required for its activity.
source: This phenotypic disparity is consistent with a model in which CofA promotes normal PBP1a function but is not absolutely required for its activity.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: PBP1a localizes to the cell pole where it is likely participating in polar surface growth.
source: PBP1a has been shown to localize to the cell pole where it is likely participating in polar surface growth (Valbuena et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PBP1a localization, supported by citation.

claim: mScar-PBP1a and mScar-CofA fusions were functional as they complemented the ampicillin hypersensitivity phenotype of the corresponding deletion allele.
source: Both fusions were functional as they complemented the ampicillin hypersensitivity phenotype of the corresponding deletion allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This validates the use of these fusions for localization studies.

claim: mScar-PBP1a displayed a prominent polar localization pattern with additional signal at developing division septa.
source: As expected based on prior results, mScar-PBP1a displayed a prominent polar localization pattern with additional signal at developing division septa (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claim: The polar localization pattern of mScar-PBP1a did not require PBP1a activity.
source: This localization pattern did not require PBP1a activity as mutant fusions inactivated for polymerase (GTase), crosslinking (TPase), or both activities retained their polar recruitment signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This demonstrates that localization is independent of enzymatic activity.

claim: mScar-CofA showed a localization pattern very similar to mScar-PBP1a.
source: mScar-CofA showed a very similar localization pattern (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claim: The polar localization pattern of mScar-CofA was lost in ΔponA cells.
source: Notably, the polar localization pattern of mScar-CofA was lost in ΔponA cells (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This suggests that CofA localization depends on PBP1a.

claim: In ΔponA cells, mScar-CofA displayed a peripheral localization signal typical of a delocalized membrane protein.
source: The fusion instead displayed a peripheral localization signal typical of a delocalized membrane protein.
evidence: This describes the localization pattern of mScar-CofA in the absence of PBP1a.

claim: The fluorescent signal of mScar-PBP1a was dramatically reduced in ΔcofA cells relative to cells producing CofA.
source: In stark contrast, when mScar-PBP1a localization was assessed in ΔcofA cells, the fluorescent signal observed was dramatically reduced relative to cells producing CofA (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claim: PBP1a may not stably accumulate in the absence of CofA.
source: This result suggested that PBP1a may not stably accumulate in the absence of CofA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced fluorescence signal.

claim: Bocillin covalently modifies the TP active site of PBPs.
source: Like all beta-lactams, Bocillin covalently modifies the TP active site of PBPs.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of Bocillin labeling.

claim: Bocillin can be used to label cellular PBPs to track their abundance in membrane extracts.
source: It can therefore be used label cellular PBPs to track their abundance in membrane extracts following protein denaturation, and separation by SDS-PAGE.
evidence: This describes the application of Bocillin labeling.

claim: The intensity of the PBP1a band was dramatically reduced in samples from ΔcofA cells compared to wild-type.
source: As expected from the fluorescent microscopy analysis, the intensity of the PBP1a band was dramatically reduced in samples from ΔcofA cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from Bocillin labeling experiments.

claim: The mScar-PBP1a band was significantly reduced in intensity when CofA was inactivated.
source: Similarly, when ΔponA cells expressing the mScar-PBP1a fusion were labeled, the PBP1a band was shifted to a higher molecular weight corresponding to the fusion, and this band was significantly reduced in intensity when CofA was inactivated (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from Bocillin labeling experiments.

claim: The effect of CofA on PBP1a levels is unlikely to be at the level of ponA transcription.
source: Given that the fusion protein was produced from a heterologous promoter, the effect of CofA is unlikely to be at the level of ponA transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: CofA is most likely required for the stable accumulation of PBP1a.
source: Rather, we infer from the data that CofA is most likely required for the stable accumulation of PBP1a.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Bocillin labeling and microscopy results.

claim: CofA interacts with PBP1a but not a control transmembrane domain fusion or PBP1b.
source: With this assay, CofA was found to interact with PBP1a but not a control transmembrane domain fusion or a fusion to PBP1b, the other aPBP encoded by Cglu (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the POLAR two-hybrid assay.

claim: CofA self-interacts.
source: Additionally, CofA was found to self interact (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the POLAR two-hybrid assay.

claim: The transmembrane domain of PBP1a is necessary and sufficient for a positive CofA-PBP1a interaction in the POLAR assay.
source: Notably, we also observed that the transmembrane domain of PBP1a was necessary and sufficient for a positive CofA-PBP1a interaction in the POLAR assay (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the POLAR two-hybrid assay.

claim: CofA interacts directly and specifically with PBP1a via its transmembrane domain.
source: We thus conclude that CofA interacts directly and specifically with PBP1a via its transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the POLAR two-hybrid assay results.

claim: Replacing the native PBP1a transmembrane domain with the corresponding domain from E. coli PBP1a resulted in accumulation of the fusion protein in ΔcofA cells.
source: Bocillin labeling indicated that unlike wild-type mScar-PBP1a, this fusion protein (mScar-EcTM-PBP1a) accumulated in ΔcofA cells to levels approaching that of the wild-type mScar-PBP1a fusion in CofA+ cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from Bocillin labeling experiments.

claim: The mScar-EcTM-PBP1a hybrid fusion was only partially functional in restoring normal levels of sensitivity to ampicillin.
source: Although accumulation of PBP1a was restored by the transmembrane domain swap, the hybrid fusion was only partially functional in restoring normal levels of sensitivity to ampicillin to ΔponA or ΔponA ΔcofA cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from drug sensitivity assays.

claim: The mScar-EcTM-PBP1a hybrid fusion was not recruited to the cell poles.
source: Moreover, the hybrid fusion was not recruited to the cell poles like wild-type mScar-PBP1a, but instead displayed a peripheral localization pattern consistent with a delocalized membrane protein (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claim: The EcTM-PBP1a hybrid failed to interact with CofA in the POLAR assay.
source: Analysis by the POLAR assay also found that the EcTM-PBP1a hybrid failed to interact with CofA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the POLAR two-hybrid assay.

claim: The CofA-PBP1a interaction is needed for the stable accumulation of the complex at the cell pole.
source: The overall results with the hybrid PBP1a fusion are therefore consistent with a model in which the CofA-PBP1a interaction is needed for the stable accumulation of the complex at the cell pole.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the results with the hybrid fusion.

claim: Proteins with the DUF3566 domain are found throughout the Actinobacteria.
source: The CofA protein from Cglu, including its two transmembrane domains, consists almost entirely of the domain of unknown function designated DUF3566. Proteins with this domain are found throughout the Actinobacteria, and as in Cglu, the cofA sequence is commonly located in the same genetic context, directly downstream of DNA gyrase and upstream of tRNA gene(s) (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This describes the distribution and genomic context of CofA homologs.

claim: The cofA sequence is commonly located directly downstream of DNA gyrase and upstream of tRNA gene(s).
source: Proteins with this domain are found throughout the Actinobacteria, and as in Cglu, the cofA sequence is commonly located in the same genetic context, directly downstream of DNA gyrase and upstream of tRNA gene(s) (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This describes the conserved genomic context of cofA.

claim: Some CofA paralogs have extended N-terminal cytoplasmic domains that may provide added functionality.
source: Some of the CofA paralogs have extended N-terminal cytoplasmic domains that may provide added functionality to the protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation about structural variation in CofA homologs.

claim: C. jeikeium CofA (CjCofA) interacts with the transmembrane domain of C. jeikeium PBP1a (CjPBP1a-TM) but not the corresponding domain of its PBP1b ortholog (CjPBP1b-TM).
source: The C. jeikium CofA (CjCofA) was found to interact with the transmembrane domain of C. jeikium PBP1a (CjPBP1a-TM), but not the corresponding domain of its PBP1b ortholog (CjPBP1b-TM) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the POLAR two-hybrid assay with C. jeikeium proteins.

claim: Full-length MtbCofA showed a weak interaction signal with the transmembrane domain of MtbPonA2 but not the transmembrane domain of MtbPonA1.
source: Using the full-length CofA from Mtb (MtbCofA-FL) as the prey, a weak interaction signal was detected with the transmembrane domain of MtbPonA2, the paralog of Cglu PBP1a, but not the transmembrane domain of MtbPonA1, the paralog of Cglu PBP1b (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the POLAR two-hybrid assay with Mtb proteins.

claim: The specific interaction signal between MtbCofA and the transmembrane domain of MtbPonA2 was greatly improved when the N-terminal extension of CofA was deleted.
source: For reasons that are currently unclear, the specific interaction signal between MtbCofA and the transmembrane domain of MtbPonA1 was greatly improved when the N-terminal extension of CofA was deleted (MtbCofA-ΔN) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a result from the POLAR two-hybrid assay with Mtb proteins.

claim: The CofA-PBP1a interaction is conserved among the Corynebacterineae and most likely also throughout the Actinobacteria.
source: We thus conclude that the CofA-PBP1a interaction is conserved among the Corynebacterineae and most likely also throughout the Actinobacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the interaction studies with proteins from different species.

claim: Cofactors of aPBPs were originally discovered in the Gram-negative bacterium Escherichia coli.
source: Cofactors of aPBPs were originally discovered in the Gram-negative bacterium Escherichia coli (Typas et al., 2010; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2010).
evidence: This is historical background about aPBP cofactors, supported by citations.

claim: In E. coli, each of the two major aPBPs, EcPBP1a and EcPBP1b, associates with a cognate outer membrane lipoprotein required for its in vivo function.
source: In this organism, each of the two major aPBPs, EcPBP1a and EcPBP1b, associates with a cognate outer membrane lipoprotein that is required for its in vivo function.
evidence: This describes the aPBP cofactor system in E. coli.

claim: EcLpoA primarily stimulates the crosslinking activity of its EcPBP1a partner.
source: Additionally, biochemical studies indicate that the EcLpoA cofactor primarily stimulates the crosslinking activity of its EcPBP1a partner, whereas the glycan polymerase activity of EcPBP1b is activated by its cofactor EcLpoB (Typas et al., 2010; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2010; Egan et al., 2014; Lupoli et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the biochemical function of EcLpoA, supported by citations.

claim: The glycan polymerase activity of EcPBP1b is activated by its cofactor EcLpoB.
source: Additionally, biochemical studies indicate that the EcLpoA cofactor primarily stimulates the crosslinking activity of its EcPBP1a partner, whereas the glycan polymerase activity of EcPBP1b is activated by its cofactor EcLpoB (Typas et al., 2010; Paradis-Bleau et al., 2010; Egan et al., 2014; Lupoli et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the biochemical function of EcLpoB, supported by citations.

claim: aPBPs in related Gram-negative bacteria require similar outer membrane lipoproteins for activity.
source: Genetic studies in related Gram-negative bacteria indicate that their aPBPs also require similar outer membrane lipoproteins for activity (Dörr et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the conservation of aPBP cofactors in Gram-negative bacteria, supported by citations.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa lacks a LpoB ortholog and PaPBP1b instead relies on the unrelated membrane lipoprotein LpoP for its function.
source: The exception is Pseudomonas aeruginosa and its relatives where a LpoB ortholog is missing and PaPBP1b instead relies on the unrelated membrane lipoprotein LpoP for its function (Greene et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes an exception to the typical aPBP cofactor system, supported by citation.

claim: aPBP cofactors are diverse and are thought to have evolved relatively recently.
source: Thus, aPBP cofactors are diverse and are thought to have evolved relatively recently (Typas et al., 2010; Typas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a general statement about aPBP cofactor evolution, supported by citations.

claim: The polytopic membrane protein CozE is essential for controlling the subcellular localization of SpPBP1a in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: The polytopic membrane protein CozE was identified as a factor that is essential for controlling the subcellular localization of SpPBP1a, whereas the bitopic membrane protein MacP was found to be required for SpPBP2a in a manner that requires phosphorylation by the Ser-Thr kinase StkP (Fenton et al., 2018; Fenton et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes aPBP cofactors in S. pneumoniae, supported by citations.

claim: The bitopic membrane protein MacP is required for SpPBP2a in a manner that requires phosphorylation by the Ser-Thr kinase StkP in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: The polytopic membrane protein CozE was identified as a factor that is essential for controlling the subcellular localization of SpPBP1a, whereas the bitopic membrane protein MacP was found to be required for SpPBP2a in a manner that requires phosphorylation by the Ser-Thr kinase StkP (Fenton et al., 2018; Fenton et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes aPBP cofactors in S. pneumoniae, supported by citations.

claim: Cofactors for aPBPs in the Actinobacteria have not been previously described prior to this study.
source: To our knowledge, cofactors for aPBPs in the Actinobacteria have not been previously described.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the CofA discovery.

claim: CofA is required for the stable accumulation of its partner enzyme PBP1a.
source: What is unique about CofA compared to other aPBP cofactors characterized previously is that it is required for the stable accumulation of its partner enzyme.
evidence: This highlights a unique feature of CofA compared to other aPBP cofactors.

claim: The accumulation defect of PBP1a in the absence of CofA is unlikely to be due to problems with transcription of the ponA gene.
source: Because the accumulation defect of PBP1a in the absence of CofA is observed when the synthase gene is expressed from a heterologous promoter, it is unlikely to be due to problems with transcription of the ponA gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The most likely explanation for the CofA-dependence for PBP1a accumulation is that the synthase is subject to proteolytic degradation in the absence of its interaction partner.
source: Instead, because components of membrane protein complexes are commonly found to depend on their partner proteins for stability (Taura et al., 1993), the most likely explanation for the CofA-dependence for PBP1a accumulation is that the synthase is subject to proteolytic degradation in the absence of its interaction partner.
evidence: This is an inference based on known principles of protein complex stability, supported by citation.

claim: Stabilized PBP1a variants that fail to interact with CofA do not localize to the cell pole.
source: Whether CofA has additional roles in PBP1a function is not clear, but the observation that stabilized PBP1a variants that fail to interact with CofA also do not localize to the cell pole suggests a role for CofA in the recruitment of PBP1a to the polar growth zones.
evidence: This is an observation that suggests an additional role for CofA.

claim: CofA may play a role in the recruitment of PBP1a to the polar growth zones.
source: Whether CofA has additional roles in PBP1a function is not clear, but the observation that stabilized PBP1a variants that fail to interact with CofA also do not localize to the cell pole suggests a role for CofA in the recruitment of PBP1a to the polar growth zones.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the localization data.

claim: A Tn-seq analysis in Mtb found that MtbCofA (Rv0007) became less dispensable in cells inactivated for its non-cognate aPBP, PonA1.
source: A Tn-seq analysis found that MtbCofA (Rv0007) became less dispensable in cells inactivated for its non-cognate aPBP, PonA1 (Kieser et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is cited evidence supporting the conserved function of CofA in Mtb.

claim: PonA1 and PonA2 have a synthetic lethal relationship in Mtb.
source: Given the synthetic lethal relationship between PonA1 and PonA2 in Mtb (Kieser et al., 2015b), this result is consistent with CofA being required for PonA2 function.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about Mtb aPBPs.

claim: A Tn-Seq study found inactivation of MtbCofA and PonA2 to both have suppressive genetic interactions with rv1565c.
source: Similarly, a different Tn-Seq study found inactivation of MtbCofA and PonA2 to both have suppressive genetic interactions with rv1565c (DeJesus et al., 2017), and a small scale phenotypic profiling screen in Mtb found that the phenotypes of MtbCofA inactivation correlated with the inactivation of PonA2 (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited evidence supporting the functional relationship between MtbCofA and PonA2.

claim: A small scale phenotypic profiling screen in Mtb found that the phenotypes of MtbCofA inactivation correlated with the inactivation of PonA2.
source: Similarly, a different Tn-Seq study found inactivation of MtbCofA and PonA2 to both have suppressive genetic interactions with rv1565c (DeJesus et al., 2017), and a small scale phenotypic profiling screen in Mtb found that the phenotypes of MtbCofA inactivation correlated with the inactivation of PonA2 (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited evidence supporting the functional relationship between MtbCofA and PonA2.

claim: MtbCofA is likely to function as an aPBP cofactor in Mtb.
source: Thus, several lines of evidence indicate that MtbCofA is likely to function as an aPBP cofactor in Mtb.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: MtbCofA has a large N-terminal extension (190 a.a.) relative to the Cglu protein.
source: Notably, MtbCofA has a large N-terminal extension (190 a.a.) relative to the Cglu protein, and this domain has been found to be a target for phosphorylation (Verma et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a structural difference in MtbCofA, with citation support for phosphorylation.

claim: The N-terminal extension of MtbCofA has been found to be a target for phosphorylation.
source: Notably, MtbCofA has a large N-terminal extension (190 a.a.) relative to the Cglu protein, and this domain has been found to be a target for phosphorylation (Verma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited evidence about post-translational modification of MtbCofA.

claim: PonA2 activity in Mtb might be controlled by phosphorylation of its cofactor.
source: Therefore, PonA2 activity in Mtb might be controlled by phosphorylation of its cofactor just as PonA1 activity is thought to be modulated by direct phosphorylation (Kieser et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the phosphorylation of MtbCofA and known regulation of PonA1.

claim: PonA1 activity is thought to be modulated by direct phosphorylation.
source: Therefore, PonA2 activity in Mtb might be controlled by phosphorylation of its cofactor just as PonA1 activity is thought to be modulated by direct phosphorylation (Kieser et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about PonA1 regulation.

claim: The localization of CofA along with its cognate aPBP at the cell pole suggests that these proteins form part of the cell elongation machinery in Actinobacteria.
source: The localization of this factor along with its cognate aPBP at the cell pole suggests that these proteins form part of the cell elongation machinery in this important group of organisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization data.
